title: Siduri the ale-wife
short: Siduri keeps a tavern at the edge of the world; Thompson's 'maker of wine' renders sabitu, which he later corrected to 'seller of wine' or 'ale-wife'.
body: In his Addenda Thompson says Siduri should perhaps be described as 'a seller of wine', reporting C. J. Gadd's suggestion 'ale-wife'. The sabitu was a woman who kept a tavern and sold beer, a familiar figure of Babylonian town life (the Laws of Hammurabi regulate her trade). Thompson's preface calls her a goddess. Thompson's note records that a Boghazköy fragment in a Hurrian dialect mentions her, and her name may itself be Hurrian. Placing a tavern-keeper at the end of the world is one of the poem's striking juxtapositions; in the Old Babylonian version she gives Gilgamish the most famous advice in the poem.

title: Siduri's veil and barred door
short: Siduri is veiled and, seeing the wild-looking stranger, bars her doors: she takes him for a violent man.
body: The meaning of the veil is debated: it may mark her divinity, her modesty, or her status as a married or respectable woman. Her fear invites the reader to see Gilgamish as others now see him: a dangerous wild man in skins, like the early Enkidu. His threat to smash her door recalls the fight at the door of the wedding-house (II) and Enkidu's speech to the cedar door (Thompson's IV, George's VII). Thompson's note on this line records that her words in thought ('one who would ravish a woman') are partly conjectural.

title: Gilgamish in animal skins
short: Clad in pelts, Gilgamish now resembles the wild Enkidu of Tablet I: his grief has reversed Enkidu's humanisation.
body: Enkidu became human by washing, oil and clothes (II). Gilgamish, mourning, has given all of these up, as Shamash foretold (VII), and has eaten the flesh of wild animals and dressed in their skins (as he tells Uta-Napishtim at the end of this tablet). Only at Uta-Napishtim's island will he be washed and newly clothed (XI). This symmetry is one of the main structural features of the late version, discussed by Tigay and George. 'Flesh of the gods' in his body yet 'woe in his belly' sums up the paradox of the two-thirds divine mourner.

anchor: who hath gone a far journey
title: The repeated questioning
short: Siduri, Ur-Shanabi and Uta-Napishtim each ask why his face is like one who has come a far road; he answers each time with the same lament.
body: The repetition is typical of the epic's style, and lets the grief for Enkidu be retold three times. The answer always includes the list of the friends' exploits (the wild ass and leopard, the Bull of Heaven, Humbaba, the lions) and ends with Enkidu's death and the question 'shall I not also lie down like him?'. Thompson faithfully keeps the verbatim repetitions, which many modern popular versions abridge. The same formula was used of the hunter in Tablet I, where his face was 'as of one who hath gone a far journey'.

title: The worm in the corpse
short: Gilgamish would not give Enkidu up for burial until decay set in; George reads that 'a maggot dropped from his nostril'.
body: Thompson's 'He like a worm hath lain on his face' is a different understanding of the line, which in modern editions describes the maggot itself falling from the corpse's nose. The image of physical decay is what turns grief into terror of death: it is the sight of corruption, not only loss, that sends Gilgamish into the wild. The worm returns in Tablet XII, where Enkidu's ghost says the worm has entered the body of the friend Gilgamish touched. The seven-day count (six days and seven nights) again marks the threshold.

title: Siduri's advice: enjoy life
short: Siduri tells Gilgamish that the gods kept life for themselves: let him feast, dance, wash, cherish his child and his wife.
body: This speech exists only in the Old Babylonian 'Sippar' tablet (published by Bruno Meissner in 1902); the standard version omits it, which Thompson's composite text does not make clear. It is the classic Mesopotamian statement of the theme later called carpe diem. The parallel with Ecclesiastes 9:7-9 ('eat thy bread with joy ... live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest') is often noted, though the resemblance is general rather than exact; scholars debate whether this reflects direct borrowing or a shared wisdom tradition. Gilgamish ignores the advice and asks only for the way to Uta-Napishtim.

title: Only the Sun crosses the ocean
short: Siduri says that only Shamash crosses the ocean: Gilgamish is attempting what only the Sun does.
body: In Babylonian belief the Sun travelled through the underworld or around the earth at night to rise again in the east. Gilgamish's journey has followed the Sun's path, through the dark tunnel of Mashu and now across the sea. The comparison expresses both his superhuman daring and the impossibility of his goal: he is not a god. Siduri's words put the journey in cosmic terms.

title: The Waters of Death
short: The Waters of Death lie between the ocean and Uta-Napishtim's land; to touch them is fatal.
body: Thompson's note suggests the idea is of the open sea beyond the tidal lagoons where the Persian Gulf meets the rivers. In Mesopotamian cosmology the earth was surrounded by a bitter ocean, beyond which lay regions no living man could reach. The Waters are a frontier between human and divine, comparable in function (not in origin) to the Styx in Greek myth. Gilgamish must cross without touching them, hence the punting poles.

title: Ur-Shanabi, the boatman
short: Ur-Shanabi is Uta-Napishtim's boatman; in the Old Babylonian text he is Sur-sunabu.
body: Thompson notes the form Sur-Sunabu in one version. The name is usually explained as 'servant of (the god) Forty', i.e. of Ea, whose sacred number was forty; the same sign was used for 'two-thirds'. He becomes Gilgamish's companion, a kind of substitute Enkidu, and returns with him to Uruk, where Gilgamish shows him the walls (XI). He is banished from the far shore for having ferried a mortal.

title: The 'sails' and the urnu: the Stone Ones
short: Gilgamish smashes things Thompson calls 'sails(?)'; modern editions read 'the Stone Ones', mysterious beings who crewed the ferry.
body: Thompson's note calls this word 'one of the greatest philological problems of the Epic', and Thompson renders the word 'sails (?)'. Later evidence has favoured that connection: George reads sut abni, 'the Stone Ones', who enabled the boat to cross the Waters of Death; by destroying them in his rage Gilgamish creates the need for the punting poles. The urnu (Thompson leaves it untranslated) is also uncertain. A typical case where Thompson's honest question-marks have been partly resolved by later finds.

title: Uta-Napishtim 'the Distant'
short: 'The Distant' is Uta-Napishtim's standing epithet: he lives at the far edge of the world.
body: Thompson's note gives a literal rendering. The epithet expresses both physical remoteness and his removal from the human condition. It recurs as a refrain in Tablet XI ('Uta-Napishtim the Distant'). Enlil's decree in XI explains it: the gods settled him 'far away, at the mouth of the rivers'. The name also carries the idea of a remote ancestor of a former age.

title: The punting poles
short: Gilgamish cuts poles five gar (about 30 m) long, knobbed with bitumen, so that he can punt across the Waters without touching them.
body: Thompson's note compares the punting-pole of southern Mesopotamia in his own day: a bamboo with a knob of bitumen at one end and a metal ring at the other. Each pole is used once and then dropped, so that Gilgamish's hand never touches the deadly water. Thompson counts 'twice-sixty' thrusts; George's text speaks of three hundred poles cut and 120 used. The scene shows the hero's endurance reduced to labour.

title: The improvised sail
short: When the poles are used up, Gilgamish makes a sail: in George's text he strips off his garment and holds it up, his arms as mast.
body: Thompson's note gives 'he completed' or 'used up his poles' as alternatives for 'ceased'. His 'set up the mast in its socket' reflects an older reading. George's version is more striking: the hero himself becomes the ship's rigging. Uta-Napishtim, watching, sees that the boat's crew is gone and a stranger aboard. Thompson's 'socket' reflects his understanding of the pole-sockets mentioned earlier.

title: Uta-Napishtim on the transience of life
short: Uta-Napishtim's answer: nothing human lasts forever, neither houses, contracts, inheritances, enmities nor the river in flood.
body: In George's fuller text the speech begins with a rebuke (Gilgamish, a king, should not behave like a fool) and moves to a meditation on human transience. The examples are from ordinary life: building, sealing documents, dividing inheritances. Thompson's fragments preserve the core of what is one of the great wisdom speeches of the poem. It is the Flood hero's first answer, before he tells his story in XI.

title: The kulilu: dragonfly, not bird
short: Thompson's 'Kulilu-bird' is read in modern editions as an insect, a dragonfly or mayfly drifting on the river: an image of brief life.
body: George translates the image of the dragonfly floating on the river, its face looking at the sun, and then suddenly nothing. Thompson, without this understanding, took the word as a bird and left the line incomplete. The modern reading turns the passage into a compact image of mortality: the flood brings the insect and its life is a moment in the sun.

title: The sleeping and the dead
short: 'The sleeping and the dead, how alike they are': no one has ever drawn the image of Death.
body: Thompson's text here is broken. In George's version the line continues that no one has depicted the form of Death, and that the free man and the slave are equal in it. The likeness of sleep and death prepares the test of Tablet XI, when Gilgamish cannot even conquer sleep. The thought links Tablets VIII, X and XI, where sleep is the image and the forerunner of death.

title: Mammitum, maker of destiny
short: Mammitum, a mother-goddess, fixes fates with the Anunnaki: they set death and life, but not the day of death.
body: The final lines of Uta-Napishtim's speech are a theology of death. Death is decreed for all; only its day is hidden. The emphasis on the gods' decree links back to Siduri's speech and forward to the story of how Uta-Napishtim himself escaped that decree, once only. Her name is related to that of the birth-goddess Mami, who in Atrahasis created mankind, so the goddess who gives life also decrees death.
